description: Alleles, genotypes, Punnett squares, cystic fibrosis, Huntington's and sex determination.
content_html:
Genes, Chromosomes and Alleles

The genome is the complete set of genetic material in an organism. In humans, DNA is packaged into 23 pairs of chromosomes inside the nucleus of most cells. Each chromosome carries hundreds of genes — sections of DNA that code for proteins. These proteins control our characteristics, from eye colour to enzyme function.

Most body cells are diploid — they carry two copies of each chromosome, one inherited from each parent. Sex cells (sperm and eggs) are haploid: they carry only one copy of each chromosome (23 in humans). At fertilisation, two haploid gametes fuse to restore the diploid number of 46.

Key Fact

Human body cells are diploid (46 chromosomes in 23 pairs). Gametes are haploid (23 chromosomes). At fertilisation, two gametes fuse to restore the diploid number of 46.

Genotype and Phenotype

Because chromosomes come in pairs, we carry two copies of each gene. Different versions of a gene are called alleles. If both alleles are identical, the individual is homozygous. If the alleles differ, the individual is heterozygous. A dominant allele (written as a capital letter, e.g. A) is expressed in the phenotype even when only one copy is present. A recessive allele (written as a lowercase letter, e.g. a) is only expressed when two copies are present (homozygous recessive).

The combination of alleles an organism carries is its genotype (e.g. Aa). The observable characteristic that results is the phenotype (e.g. brown eyes). The phenotype depends on which alleles are present and how they interact.

Key Fact

Dominant alleles are expressed even in one copy; recessive alleles are only expressed when two copies are present. Genotype = allele combination; phenotype = observable characteristic produced.

Punnett Squares

A Punnett square is used to predict the possible genotypes and phenotypes of offspring from a genetic cross. Place one parent’s alleles along the top and the other parent’s alleles down the side. Fill each box by combining one allele from each parent.

Example: two heterozygous parents (Bb × Bb), where B (brown coat) is dominant over b (white coat). The possible offspring genotypes are BB, Bb, Bb and bb — giving a 3:1 phenotype ratio (three brown : one white). As probabilities: 75% chance of the dominant phenotype, 25% chance of the recessive phenotype. These are expected ratios, not guaranteed outcomes — chance means actual results may differ, especially with small samples.

A full genetic diagram includes: (1) parental phenotypes and genotypes; (2) gametes produced by each parent; (3) a 2×2 Punnett square; (4) offspring genotypes with phenotypes stated; (5) probabilities or ratios. Always show gametes as a separate step — examiners expect this. State the phenotype of each offspring genotype, not just the allele letters. If only one parent is heterozygous (e.g. Bb × bb), the offspring ratio is 1:1 (50% Bb, 50% bb), meaning half show the dominant phenotype and half show the recessive phenotype.

Inherited Disorders

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. A person must inherit two copies of the faulty allele (ff) to have the condition. Individuals with one copy (Ff) are carriers — they carry the allele but show no symptoms. When two carriers have children, there is a 25% chance each child will have cystic fibrosis, a 50% chance each child will be a carrier, and a 25% chance each child will be unaffected and not a carrier. Cystic fibrosis causes thick, sticky mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system, impairing breathing and digestion.

Huntington’s disease is caused by a dominant allele (H). Only one copy is needed for the condition to appear, so a heterozygous individual (Hh) will develop it. This means an affected parent with genotype Hh has a 50% chance of passing the condition to each child, even if the other parent is unaffected (hh). Huntington’s causes progressive deterioration of the nervous system, with symptoms typically appearing in mid-adulthood.

Sex is determined by the 23rd pair of chromosomes. Females have two X chromosomes (XX); males have one X and one Y (XY). Because fathers can pass either an X or a Y chromosome in their sperm, there is a 50:50 probability that each child will be female (XX) or male (XY). This can be shown with a Punnett square using X and Y instead of allele letters.

Embryo screening can be used to test embryos produced by IVF for specific genetic disorders before implantation. This is called pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD). It raises ethical questions: supporters argue it prevents suffering; critics argue it raises issues about designer babies and the potential for selecting non-medical traits. Genetic testing of adults can also identify carriers before they have children, allowing informed decisions about family planning.

Key Fact

Cystic fibrosis (recessive, ff): both parents must be carriers for a 25% risk per child. Huntington’s disease (dominant, H): one affected parent (Hh × hh) gives a 50% risk per child. Sex: XX = female, XY = male.
exam_tip_html: For genetic diagram questions, always show your working in full: parental phenotypes, parental genotypes, gametes (circled or listed separately), Punnett square, and offspring phenotypes with ratios or percentages. Missing any step loses marks even if the final ratio is correct. For a ‘3 marks — Explain’ question on cystic fibrosis, state that it is caused by a recessive allele, explain that carriers have one copy and are unaffected, and give the 25% probability when two carriers have children. For Huntington’s disease, state clearly that it is dominant so only one copy causes the condition. Never confuse dominant with ‘common’ — a dominant allele can still be rare in the population.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Alleles are different versions of a gene. Dominant alleles are expressed in one copy; recessive alleles only show when two copies are present. Genotype is the allele combination; phenotype is the observable result.
  • Punnett squares predict offspring genotype and phenotype ratios from a cross. Crossing two heterozygotes (Bb × Bb) gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio as a probability — not a guarantee.
  • Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (25% risk if both parents are carriers). Huntington’s disease is caused by a dominant allele (50% risk if one parent is affected). Sex is determined by the X and Y chromosomes: XX = female, XY = male.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes a heterozygous genotype for a gene with alleles A and a?
A) AA
B) Aa
C) aa
D) AB
State what is meant by the term phenotype.
practice_questions.marks:
The observable characteristics of an organism [1 mark]
Accept: the physical appearance of an organism produced by its genotype (and environment)

practice_questions.text:
Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). Two carrier parents (Ff) have a child.
Describe the possible genotypes of the child and state the probability of the child having cystic fibrosis.
practice_questions.marks:
Possible genotypes: FF, Ff, ff [1 mark for identifying all three]
Probability of cystic fibrosis (ff): 25% (or 1 in 4 / 1:4) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Huntington's disease is caused by a dominant allele (H). A parent with genotype Hh has children with an unaffected partner (hh).
Explain why 50% of their children are expected to develop Huntington's disease. Include a genetic diagram in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Parental genotypes: Hh × hh [1 mark]
Gametes shown: H and h from affected parent; h and h from unaffected parent [1 mark]
Offspring: Hh (affected) and hh (unaffected) in 1:1 ratio, so 50% probability of Hh offspring developing the condition; stated because the H allele is dominant so one copy causes disease [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A student has data from crossing two heterozygous plants (Tt × Tt), where T (tall) is dominant over t (dwarf).
Calculate the expected percentage of tall plants in the offspring.
practice_questions.marks:
Parental genotypes: Tt × Tt [1 mark]
Gametes: T and t from each parent [1 mark]
Punnett square completed correctly: TT, Tt, Tt, tt [1 mark]
Tall offspring (TT + Tt) = 3 out of 4 = 75% [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of embryo screening to test for inherited genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis before implantation during IVF.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation with developed points for and against, clear explanation of how the technique works, and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Arguments on both sides with some development; may lack full explanation of the technique or conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points on one or both sides with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement with little or no evaluation.

Points may include:
For: prevents suffering of children born with serious conditions; allows families at risk to have unaffected biological children; reduces pressure on NHS caring for affected individuals.
Against: raises concerns about selecting embryo characteristics beyond medical need; some argue unused embryos are destroyed, raising ethical objections; risk of social pressure on parents to select; may lead to reduced acceptance of people with disabilities.
Conclusion should weigh severity of condition against ethical concerns.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of allele is only expressed in the phenotype when two copies are present?
Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. If both parents are carriers (Ff), what is the probability of having a child with cystic fibrosis?
A Punnett square crossing two heterozygous parents (Bb × Bb) produces a phenotype ratio of _____.
Sex is determined by the 23rd pair of chromosomes. Females have _____ and males have XY.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: The allele combination an organism carries
Having two identical alleles for a gene

flashcard_questions.a: A different version of the same gene.
Having two identical alleles for a particular gene (e.g. AA or aa).
Having two different alleles for a particular gene (e.g. Aa).

flashcard_questions.q: How many chromosomes do human body cells contain?
How many chromosomes do human gametes contain?
What phenotype ratio does a Bb × Bb cross produce?
What type of allele causes cystic fibrosis — dominant or recessive?
flashcard_questions.a: Recessive — both copies must be faulty (ff) for the condition to appear.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the probability of cystic fibrosis when both parents are carriers (Ff)?
What type of allele causes Huntington's disease?
flashcard_questions.a: Dominant — one copy (Hh) is enough to cause the condition.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the probability of Huntington's disease from a Hh × hh cross?
flashcard_questions.a: 50% — half the offspring will be Hh (affected).

flashcard_questions.q: What sex chromosomes do females have? What do males have?

glossary_terms.definition: The entire set of genetic material (DNA) in an organism, containing all the genes needed to build and maintain it.
Thread-like structures made of DNA, found in the nucleus. Humans have 23 pairs (46 in total).
Short sections of DNA on a chromosome that code for specific proteins, determining particular characteristics.
Different versions of the same gene. For example, the gene for eye colour may have a brown allele and a blue allele.
Having two identical alleles for a particular gene — either both dominant (AA) or both recessive (aa).
Having two different alleles for a particular gene, for example one dominant and one recessive (Aa).
The genetic makeup of an organism, described using letters to represent alleles (e.g. Aa, AA, aa).
The observable characteristics of an organism, determined by both its genotype and its environment.
A genetic disease caused by a recessive allele, where both copies of the gene must be faulty for the condition to appear. Carriers have one copy but are unaffected.
A genetic disorder caused by a dominant allele, causing progressive damage to the nervous system. Only one copy of the allele is needed to develop the condition.
